newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Strong SAfrica trade balance seen boosting '97 BoP.
newsitem.headline: Strong SAfrica trade balance seen boosting '97 BoP.

text.p: A surprising jump in South Africa's December trade surplus to more than two billion rand ($432.8 million) suggests that the balance of payments will improve strongly this year, economists said on Thursday.

Figures released earlier showed the country's trade surplus leaping to 2.04 billion rand in the last month of 1996, well above a Reuters consensus estimate of 760 million rand and a 378-million rand surplus in November.
December's data helped boost the year's surplus to 10.577 billion rand, more than double 1995's total of 4.884 billion rand.
"The (December) figure was a major surprise on the upside," said Dave Mohr, chief economist at life assurer Old Mutual.

Though trade data are notoriously volatile, and the December figure could have been helped by a low level of imports at year end, the trend in the last few months of 1996 had been towards bigger surpluses, economists said.
And they said they expected this trend to continue during 1997, though at a slower rate than in fourth-quarter 1996.
"The expectation for most people is that imports will start slowing down and exports start to do better," said Kevin Lings, senior economist at UAL Merchant Bank.

Exports were seen gaining momentum as the effects of the weaker rand, which lost 29 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar during 1996, fed through. Imports were expected to taper off amid an expected economic slowdown, economists said.
Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals told Reuters on Wednesday that he expected economic growth to slow to around two percent in 1997 from some three percent in 1996.
Economists said a healthier trade balance this year would help rebuild the country's low reserves, which had made the rand a target for speculative attacks.
"The current account is starting to improve, stabilising the rand. Obviously, capital flows are still volatile but at least the source of pressure on the rand seems to be easing," Mohr said.
Together with Stals' upbeat comments on Wednesday, a more bullish economic outlook for South Africa is seen this year.

Stals said on Wednesday he saw scope for a "very stable" rand in 1997, with the currency depreciating less than the inflation differentials between South Africa and its major trading partners. He put the differential between seven and eight percent.

Stals forecasted the current account of the balance of payments at about half of 1996's deficit, which he estimated at about 10 billion rand. Consumer inflation should average less than 10 percent, he said.
"Some of the pieces of jigsaw puzzle are falling into place, even though we don't have all yet," Mohr said.
